name: CEDNIK syndrome
aliases: cerebral dysgenesis, neuropathy, ichthyosis and keratoderma syndrome

clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive neurocutaneous syndrome whose acronym captures cerebral dysgenesis, neuropathy, ichthyosis and keratoderma
Caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SNAP29, a SNARE protein required for vesicle fusion, autophagy and lamellar-body secretion in keratinocytes
Cutaneous features include generalised ichthyosis with a palmoplantar keratoderma, reflecting defective epidermal barrier lipid delivery
Neurological involvement is prominent, with structural brain malformations such as agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, polymicrogyria, developmental delay and peripheral neuropathy
Facial dysmorphism, feeding difficulties and failure to thrive are commonly reported
Diagnosis rests on the combination of ichthyosis and keratoderma with neuroimaging abnormalities, confirmed by SNAP29 molecular testing
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, combining emollients and keratolytics with neurological, developmental and nutritional care
reference.pathophysiology: CEDNIK syndrome results from loss of function of SNAP29, a soluble NSF attachment protein receptor (SNARE) that mediates fusion of intracellular vesicles and participates in autophagy. In the epidermis, SNAP29 is required for the secretion of lamellar bodies that deliver barrier lipids to the stratum corneum, so its deficiency disrupts keratinocyte maturation and produces ichthyosis and palmoplantar keratoderma. The same defect in vesicular trafficking during nervous system development underlies the cerebral dysgenesis and peripheral neuropathy that characterise the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital ichthyoses with neurological involvement
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI for corpus callosum dysgenesis, cortical malformation and other structural anomalies
Nerve conduction studies for peripheral neuropathy
Skin biopsy with ultrastructural study of lamellar-body secretion
redFlags: Severe feeding difficulty with failure to thrive and aspiration risk
Recurrent skin or systemic infection compromising an impaired barrier
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is guarded and dominated by the severity of the cerebral malformation and neurological impairment; many affected children have significant developmental disability, while the cutaneous features are chronic but manageable.
pitfalls: Focusing on the ichthyosis and keratoderma without arranging neuroimaging
Mistaking the syndrome for an isolated congenital ichthyosis and missing the neurological diagnosis
Underestimating feeding and nutritional needs in an infant with neurological impairment
Failing to offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition
management: No disease-specific therapy; care is supportive and multidisciplinary
Skin-directed care with emollients, keratolytics and topical retinoids for the ichthyosis and palmoplantar keratoderma
Nutritional support and management of feeding difficulties and failure to thrive, with gastrostomy where needed
Antiseizure treatment, physiotherapy and developmental support for the encephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy
Attention to secondary infection of fissured keratoderma with ongoing barrier care
Ophthalmology, orthopaedic and other specialist input as complications arise
Genetic counselling and family testing for the autosomal recessive SNAP29 variant
